opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly I think it's still a pretty open area. Most of what people call multi-agent systems today is really the same general-purpose model, prompted in different ways, with some orchestration code around it: one instance plans, another writes code, another critiques. That works surprisingly well, but the models weren't trained with that setup in mind. They were trained to be helpful single assistants talking to a human.

So the opportunity I see is in closing that gap. A few things come to mind.

First, communication. When two LLM agents talk to each other, they tend to be very verbose. They're polite, they restate context, they hedge. That's fine for a human reader but wasteful between agents. You could imagine fine-tuning, or doing reinforcement learning, so that models learn to pass along exactly the information the other agent needs. That means shorter messages, more structured handoffs, and fewer tokens and less latency overall.

Second, role specialization. Right now we mostly rely on a system prompt saying "you are the reviewer." But you could train smaller, specialized models for particular roles. A verifier model that's really good at catching errors is a different skill from a generator that's good at proposing solutions. We already see a version of this with reward models and verifiers in reasoning training, and I think extending that into deliberate agent roles makes a lot of sense, partly because a smaller specialized model can be much cheaper to run.

Third, and probably the hardest, is credit assignment. If you train with reinforcement learning on a multi-agent task and the final answer is wrong, which agent made the mistake? Was it the planner, the tool call, or the summarizer that dropped an important detail? That's a classic problem from multi-agent RL, and it shows up again here. Methods that give more fine-grained feedback, like process-level rewards or per-step verification, will probably matter a lot.

And then there's robustness. Agents need to learn when not to trust another agent's output. If one agent hallucinates and the next one just accepts it, errors compound. Training models to be appropriately skeptical, to check claims and ask for clarification, is something single-assistant training doesn't really emphasize.

That said, I'd add a bit of caution. Often a single strong model with good tools and a longer reasoning budget does as well as or better than an elaborate multi-agent setup. So I think the real opportunity is in figuring out when multiple agents actually help, for example through parallelism, separation of concerns, or independent verification, and then training specifically for those cases, rather than adding agents for the sake of it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think that's a really interesting question, and it's something I've been thinking about quite a bit. Right now, most LLMs are trained essentially as standalone models. You have pretraining, then instruction fine-tuning, then some kind of preference tuning with RLHF or DPO or whatever variant. But all of that is really optimized for a single model talking to a single user. Nobody is really training the model with the expectation that its output is going to be consumed by another model, or that it's going to have to coordinate with other agents that might have different information or different roles.

And I think that's a gap, because in practice, when people build these multi-agent systems today, they take an off-the-shelf model and they just prompt it into a role. "You are the planner," "you are the critic," "you are the executor." It works surprisingly well, but it's kind of brittle. The models were never trained to, say, hand off a task cleanly, or to recognize when they should defer to another agent, or to communicate in a way that is actually efficient for another model rather than for a human reader. A lot of what passes between agents right now is very verbose natural language, because that's what the model learned to produce. There's probably a lot of room to make that communication more compact and more reliable.

So one concrete opportunity I see is in the fine-tuning stage. You could imagine collecting trajectories from multi-agent setups, filtering for the ones that actually succeed, and then fine-tuning on those, similar to what people do with rejection sampling or STaR-style approaches for reasoning. The reward signal there is interesting because it's a group outcome, not an individual one. That's kind of the classic credit assignment problem from multi-agent reinforcement learning, and I don't think the LLM community has really engaged with that literature much yet.

The other thing I find interesting is specialization. Right now we tend to use the same big model for every role, which is wasteful. If you know a model is only ever going to be the tool-calling executor, it probably doesn't need to be a 400-billion-parameter model. You could train smaller, more specialized models for specific roles in the system, and I think that's where some of the practical cost benefits will come from. It's a bit like the mixture-of-experts idea but at the system level rather than inside a single forward pass.

I'd also be a little cautious, though. There's a tendency to get excited about agents and multi-agent systems and to overlook that a lot of the gains people report are from better prompting or better scaffolding, not from the model itself being different. So before training specifically for multi-agent settings, I'd want to see clearer evidence of where the single-model approach actually breaks down. But I do think, as these systems get more complex and the interactions get longer, training for the multi-agent setting is going to become necessary rather than just a nice-to-have.

r001.rationale: The response says current LLMs are trained for single-user interaction, not to coordinate with other agents, and that multi-agent systems use off-the-shelf models prompted into roles.

r002.rationale: It proposes fine-tuning on successful multi-agent trajectories as a concrete opportunity to train models for these settings.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss hosted LLM users or their dependence on providers to perform specialized training.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a real opportunity there, because right now we mostly train models to be useful individually, and then we put them into a system where they’re supposed to collaborate. Those are somewhat different objectives. Being good at answering a question doesn’t necessarily mean being good at deciding when to ask another model for help, what information to share, or when to challenge another model’s answer.

You could imagine training on tasks where the reward depends on the outcome of the whole group. Then the models could learn how to divide up the work and communicate effectively. And I think an important part would be learning when collaboration is actually useful. If one model can solve the problem, having five models discuss it might just add cost and latency.

The challenging part is figuring out whether you’re getting a real benefit from collaboration. Are the models contributing different information and catching each other’s mistakes, or are they just agreeing with each other? I’d want to compare that against giving a single model the same computational budget. But that ability to learn how to work together, instead of relying entirely on us to prescribe the interaction, seems like a promising direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of opportunity there, because right now we usually take a model that was trained to be a helpful assistant and then put it into a system with other agents. But being good at answering a user’s question doesn’t necessarily mean you’re good at collaborating.

For example, an agent needs to recognize when it should solve something itself, when it should delegate, and what information another agent needs. And then there’s the question of checking each other’s work. If you have five agents and they all make the same mistake, you haven’t really gained much by having five of them.

So I think an interesting direction is training on the interaction itself, where the reward depends on whether the group successfully completes a task. You could potentially get agents that specialize in different roles, but also learn when to ask for help or challenge an answer.

The important question for me would be whether that actually gives you better performance than spending the same compute on one model. More agents means more communication and more tokens. So I’d want to compare those approaches under the same budget and see where collaboration really helps.
